chapter: Tenor players, tours and band boys
title: Touring Japan with Sam Taylor, a star after Harlem Nocturne
summary: He played 72 cities in Japan with Sam Taylor, who was the biggest name there after the Beatles.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Yeah, and you also went to Japan with Sam Taylor a couple of times, didn't you?

Oh, I went with Sam Taylor five times to Japan. In fact, I played 72 cities in Japan -- one time we were there for 6 weeks, and we played from the top, north, from Wakinai all the way down to Nakasaki -- 72 cities. I never worked that hard in my life! Other than working with Lionel Hampton.
Tell me about Sam's great success in Japan.

Well, the funny thing, you know -- Sam recorded Harlem Nocturne for MGM Records here in New York, and they sent the record over to Japan, and it became an instant sensation over there; he was the biggest musician in Japan. All of the tenor saxaphone players tried to get the same sound and tried to breathe and play exactly like he did. I mean, this man was really a big star; in fact, the only people that outdrew him in Japan were the Beatles. He was the second

biggest name in Japan.
And he had a lot of success there, and people
really loved him there.

Yeah, Sam did have tremendous success,
and it certainly is nice to hear that about Sam Taylor in
Japan. And he probably opened the way for a lot of other guys
because ...

Yes he did, Syl Austin and all those
other guys got a chance to go over there.

Yeah, a lot of guys were going to Japan
and doing very well. I know of many people going over there.
I was there with Louie Armstrong many years back, and I really
enjoyed that country very much.
Yeah, I love it over there, too.
